messages.author: 7d2a96af532ed7de
messages.subject: Phonegap
parts:
Hello Folks!

I've been wondering recently if it's possible to use Phonegap (http://phonegap.com/), to package a Shiny app into a little  for use on iOS, Android etc.

As far as I understand Phonegap, it's basically just a wrapper around something which launches a web page in the native browser. It also has some additional features for notifications, etc.

I haven't done any work on it yet, but I was just wondering if anyone else had had a go, or if they know of any technical reasons why it might be problematic or a bad idea.

Best,

Brendan

messages.author: bbc57ffa8a14ad13
messages.subject: Re: Phonegap
parts:
I spent some time on this a while back. Here's what I recall from my investigating:
  1. I think the idea is doable, but there are a few awkward hacks.
  2. Some of the difficulties come from using a load-balanced system like Shiny Server Pro or ShinyApps.io. I think you'd be better off -- at least for a proof-of-concept -- connecting to a single-process model like Shiny Server Open Source.
  3. PhoneGap Build is a competent enough platform -- ingests PhoneGap projects and products iPhone/Android/Windows/whatever packages. It's one more thing to learn/distrust, so I don't know that I'd recommend it for your "Hello World," but once you're ready to actually bundle something for multiple platforms, it's pretty nice.
  4. There are some really awkward bits around what to bundle and what not to bundle. The idea of PhoneGap, of course, is that you could save all your static assets within your application bundle and then only connect to a server when necessary. This becomes complicated with the various ways that Shiny presents static assets and allows packages to extend those sets of static assets. It's tough to make sure you have everything downloaded locally, so you're probably better off just loading the base HTML file remotely. I had a hard time convincing PhoneGap Build to do this, though it looks like it is possible to do in PhoneGap itself. Note that this becomes difficult with point 6.
  5. The persistent connection assumption of Shiny is awkward for a mobile device. When the WebSocket connection drops (which I'm sure depends on the platform/phone), you get the familiar gray screen covering your app. This is pretty awkward and hard for an app to recover from.
  6. PhoneGap works by referencing a phonegap.js file in the code that you write to expose the PhoneGap API. Then when you compile, it replaces that file with the version relevant to your targeted platform. This clashes with my simplifying suggestion in point 4, in that if you're loading all the files remotely, then you can't have the PhoneGap build process replace your phonegap.js file with the one you actually need on that platform. There are ways around this in PhoneGap I believe, but I couldn't get any working when trying to load the files from a remote URL.
  7. You still need to write the JavaScript integration between the PhoneGap API and Shiny. I had one or two of these working just to prove the concept, but it's work to be done.
So it's certainly possible to create a mobile app that just shows a remote URL (like ShinyApps) but there's a big jump between that and integrating the PhoneGap API to actually use the phone's capabilities.

I'm certainly not a PhoneGap expert, so I may have missed something obvious, and I don't know how valuable I'd be as a resource moving forward beyond what I've outlined in the above points, but feel free to ask if you have particular questions and I'll see if I remember.

Jeff
